passage:
Saturday. Rehan, ten, showed his little sister Farida how to make a paper boat. Fold, fold, flip, pull, done. "See? Easy." Farida, five, held a crumpled square and started to cry. "You're not even trying!" Rehan snapped, and went off to play.
Sunday. Rehan tried again, faster, and louder. Farida hid her paper under the sofa. Their neighbour Nandini aunty, watching from the door, asked, "Rehan, who taught you?" He thought. "Abbu. It took ages. I kept tearing mine."
Wednesday. Rehan sat on the floor with two sheets. "First fold it in half like a book. Show me. Good. Now the corners down, like a roof." He waited at every step. Farida's boat came out lopsided. She floated it in a bucket, shrieking with joy.

qa.q: How did Rehan explain the first fold on Wednesday?
qa.a: "First fold it in half like a book."

qa.q: Why did Rehan snap at Farida on Saturday?
qa.a: The folds felt so easy to him that he couldn't imagine them being hard, so he thought she wasn't trying and got frustrated.

qa.q: What changed in Rehan's teaching, and why did it work?
qa.a: He broke it into small steps, waited at each one and checked her fold, which gave Farida time to follow.

qa.q: What was Saturday like for Farida?
qa.a: She was left holding a crumpled square while her brother rushed through, which made her feel she couldn't do it, and she cried. 😢

grounding: It shows an older brother skipping steps that feel obvious to him and getting angry when his little sister is lost.

passage: Come, sit near your Seema Ammachi. You're cross with your little cousin because he can't follow your game? Let me tell you about your Appa, Jomon, when he was nine. He tried to teach his little brother Tomy to ride the old black cycle in our courtyard. Jomon just said, "Sit, pedal, balance, go!" and pushed. Tomy fell into the jasmine bush. Jomon threw up his hands. "Why can't you do it? It's so simple!" He had forgotten that he himself fell off that cycle for a whole month. To him, balance was just there, like breathing. Tomy was crying and Jomon was angry, both in the same courtyard. Only when your Appachan held the seat and walked beside Tomy, slowly, did the boy learn.

qa.q: Where did Tomy fall?
qa.a: Into the jasmine bush.

qa.q: Why did Jomon think riding was so simple?
qa.a: Jomon felt frustrated because he could already balance without thinking, like breathing, and had forgotten falling off that cycle for a whole month himself.

qa.q: How did Appachan's way of teaching fix the problem?
qa.a: He held the seat and walked beside Tomy slowly, giving support step by step instead of expecting instant balance.

qa.q: Why might Seema Ammachi be telling this story now?
qa.a: The grandchild is cross with a little cousin who can't follow a game, and Ammachi wants them to see how easy things look once you already know them.

grounding: It shows an older brother who skips the steps of riding that feel obvious to him and grows angry when his little brother falls.

passage:
The power went out at seven, and Disha's maths homework was due the next morning. Anand, eleven, sat with her by a candle on the dining table. "Fifty-two minus eighteen. Easy. Borrow, then thirty-four."
Disha, seven, blinked at the page. "Borrow what?"
"From the five! Obviously." Anand wrote 34 and tapped it. "Done."
"But how?"
"I just told you!" His voice rose. The candle flickered. Disha pushed the notebook away and put her head down on her arms.
Anand stared at the flame, annoyed. It was so clear in his head that he couldn't see what was missing. Then Mummy called from the kitchen, "Do it with matchsticks, like your teacher did with you."
Matchsticks. He'd forgotten he ever needed them.

qa.q: What sum was in Disha's homework?
qa.a: Fifty-two minus eighteen.

qa.q: Why did Anand think his explanation was enough?
qa.a: Anand felt annoyed because borrowing was so clear in his head that he couldn't see which steps Disha was missing, and he'd forgotten he once needed matchsticks himself.

qa.q: How could Anand use the matchsticks to help Disha?
qa.a: He could show fifty-two as five bundles of ten and two loose sticks, open one bundle to take eighteen away, and let Disha count what is left.

qa.q: What was it like for Disha when Anand said "I just told you!"?
qa.a: She felt lost and a bit shamed, which is why she pushed the notebook away and put her head down.

grounding: It shows an older brother, during a power cut, skipping steps that feel obvious to him and getting frustrated when his sister is lost.

passage:
On the carrom board in their Hyderabad flat, Faisal, eleven, lined up the striker for his little sister Ayesha. "Okay. Just flick it off the side and cut the white into the corner."
Ayesha, six, flicked. The striker spun off the board and under the sofa.
"No! Cut it. Off the side. It's easy." He did it himself in one smooth shot. Click, into the pocket. "See?"
Ayesha tried again. The striker barely moved.
"Why aren't you listening?" Faisal's voice got loud. "I've told you twice!"
Keerthana from next door, watching from the doorway, said, "Faisal, she doesn't even know how to hold her fingers yet."
Faisal opened his mouth to argue, then looked at Ayesha's hand, flat on the board with her thumb sticking out, and went quiet.

qa.q: Where did the striker go when Ayesha first flicked it?
qa.a: It spun off the board and under the sofa.

qa.q: Why does Faisal get so frustrated with Ayesha?
qa.a: The shot is so easy for Faisal that he can't remember not knowing it, so he thinks she isn't listening when she is actually missing the first steps.

qa.q: What turning point came for Faisal, and what could he do next?
qa.a: Looking at Ayesha's flat hand after Keerthana spoke; he could start by showing her how to hold her fingers before any cut shots.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see the lesson from the doorway?
qa.a: Keerthana can see what Faisal can't: Ayesha is missing the very first step, and the shouting is only making her more lost.

grounding: It shows an older boy teaching his little sister carrom, skipping steps that seem obvious to him, and getting frustrated when she is lost.

passage:
"Kavitha, look. Big hand on twelve, small hand on four. Four o'clock. Done. Now what time is this?"
"Um... six?"
"No! The small hand is on six, the big hand is on six too. So half past... no, six-thirty. Obviously."
"Anna, why is it half?"
"Because it's on the six. I'm not explaining again."
"But you said six means six!"
"Amma! She's not trying!"
Shalini came in drying her hands. "Karthik, when did you learn clocks?"
"I don't know. Always?"
"You learned in Class 2, and you cried for a week. Tell her what the big hand does first. Just the big hand."
Karthik sighed, then pointed. "Okay. This one is the minute hand. It goes all the way round in one hour."

qa.q: What time did Karthik show first?
qa.a: Four o'clock, with the big hand on twelve and the small hand on four.

qa.q: Why does Karthik think Kavitha is not trying?
qa.a: Reading a clock feels like something he has always known, so he skips why the six can mean half past and blames her when she gets lost.

qa.q: What choice by Amma turned the lesson around?
qa.a: Reminding Karthik that he once struggled too, and telling him to start with only the big hand, so he begins from the step Kavitha is missing.

qa.q: What is it like for Kavitha when Karthik says six means half past?
qa.a: It is confusing and a little upsetting, because he first said the number meant the hour, and now the same number means something else and she is being scolded for it.

grounding: It shows an older boy teaching his little sister the clock, skipping steps that seem obvious to him and getting frustrated when she is lost.

passage:
Monday. Bhupen, eleven, had promised Aai he'd teach his little brother Omkar to tie shoelaces before school started. "Loop, wrap, pull. Done." He did it in two seconds. Omkar stared at the tangle in his own fingers. "Again!" Bhupen did it faster. Omkar's lip wobbled. "You're not even trying!" Bhupen shouted, and stomped off.
Wednesday. Bhupen watched Aai teach Omkar a song, one line at a time, waiting after each. He thought about his own shoelaces. When had he learned? He couldn't remember not knowing.
Saturday. Bhupen sat on the step with Omkar and one big shoe. "First, make a bunny ear. Just one. Show me." He waited. "Now the other lace goes round the ear like a scarf." It took twenty minutes and three restarts. When the bow held, Omkar shrieked. Bhupen grinned even wider than his brother.

qa.q: What had Bhupen promised Aai?
qa.a: He had promised to teach his little brother Omkar to tie shoelaces before school started.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen get so frustrated on Monday?
qa.a: Bhupen felt impatient and angry, because tying laces seemed so obvious to him that he couldn't see how many steps Omkar was missing.

qa.q: What changed in Bhupen's teaching on Saturday, and why did it work?
qa.a: He broke it into one small step at a time, a bunny ear first, and waited for Omkar to show him, just as Aai did with the song.

qa.q: What was Monday like for Omkar?
qa.a: Omkar felt lost and close to tears, watching the laces flash by in two seconds and then being shouted at.

grounding: Shows an older child skipping steps that seem obvious to him while teaching his little brother, then learning to slow down.

passage: Vidya, you're cross that your little brother can't learn long division from you? Sit. Your Dada Chetan was just the same. When I was ten, I tried to teach my sister Kamla to ride my old cycle in the lane behind the mill. I'd been riding for years. I said, "Just pedal and balance, it's easy!" and let go. She fell. I said it again, louder, and let go again. She fell again and scraped her knee. I got so angry I threw my cap on the ground. My father had watched all of this, and he asked me, "Chetan, do you remember your first day?" I didn't. I couldn't remember ever not knowing. So he said, "Then start where she is." Next morning I held the seat and ran beside her, one pedal at a time. By Sunday she was racing me.

qa.q: Where did young Chetan try to teach Kamla to ride?
qa.a: In the lane behind the mill.

qa.q: Why did young Chetan get so angry when Kamla kept falling?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and angry because riding felt so easy to him that he couldn't imagine not knowing how to balance, so her falling seemed like not trying.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Dada's story?
qa.a: His father asking whether he remembered his first day and telling him to start where she is; next morning Chetan held the seat and went one pedal at a time.

qa.q: What might those first attempts have been like for Kamla?
qa.a: Kamla was probably scared and sore, being let go again and again and scraping her knee while her brother shouted.

grounding: Shows an older child skipping steps that seem obvious while teaching a younger sister, and getting frustrated when she is lost.

passage: The wedding band in the next building had started, drums thumping through the window, and Zaid's subtraction homework was due in the morning. Ammi was at work till nine. "Asif, help him," she had said on the phone. Asif, twelve, looked at the first sum: 52 minus 27. "Easy. Seven from two, can't, so borrow, twelve minus seven is five, four minus two is two. Twenty-five." Zaid's pencil hung in the air. "Borrow from where?" "From the five! Obviously!" The drums got louder. Zaid's eyes filled. Asif slammed the book shut. Then he remembered his own teacher bundling matchsticks into tens with a rubber band. He grabbed the matchbox from the kitchen. "Okay. Five bundles of ten, and two loose ones. You need seven loose. What do we do?" Zaid stared, then slowly untied a bundle.

qa.q: What was the first subtraction sum?
qa.a: The first sum was 52 minus 27.

qa.q: Why did Asif slam the book shut?
qa.a: Asif felt frustrated and pressured by the drums and the deadline, and borrowing seemed so obvious that Zaid's confusion felt like not trying.

qa.q: What made Asif's second try work better?
qa.a: Using bundles of matchsticks showed where the ten comes from, one step at a time, and let Zaid work it out instead of hearing the answer fast.

qa.q: What was it like for Zaid when Asif rattled off the steps?
qa.a: Zaid felt lost and upset, with no idea where 'borrow' came from, his eyes filling as the drums got louder.

grounding: Shows an older child racing through steps that seem obvious while helping his little brother, and slowing down with matchsticks under time pressure.

passage: On the colony road in Jalandhar, Manoj was teaching his little brother Joseph to ride a bicycle. Manoj had ridden for five years; it felt like breathing. "Just pedal and balance," he said. Joseph wobbled and fell. "Pedal AND balance!" Manoj said louder. Joseph fell again. "It's so easy, why can't you do it?" Joseph's lip trembled. "You didn't tell me how to balance." Manoj opened his mouth, then closed it. How did he balance? He didn't know. He just did. Their mother came out and said, "Remember, Manoj, you took a whole summer to learn. Papa held the seat." Manoj had completely forgotten. He knelt down. "Okay. Look ahead, not at the wheel. I'll hold the seat and run." Joseph sniffed and got back on.

qa.q: How long had Manoj been riding a bicycle?
qa.a: Manoj had ridden for five years.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when Joseph kept falling?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and impatient, because riding felt so easy to him that he couldn't see why Joseph was struggling.

qa.q: What did Manoj change after his mother's reminder?
qa.a: He gave a clear small step, look ahead and not at the wheel, and held the seat while running.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel when Manoj said it was so easy?
qa.a: Joseph felt hurt and discouraged, his lip trembling, because nobody had explained how to balance.

grounding: Shows an older child teaching his younger brother to ride, skipping steps that feel obvious to him and getting frustrated when the little one struggles.

passage:
"Bhavna, it's simple. You can't take seven from two, so you borrow."
"Borrow what?"
"From the next number. Obviously."
"Why?"
"Because you have to! Just do it."
"I don't understand, Jagdish bhaiya."
"Ugh, how don't you understand? It's so easy!"
"You're shouting."
"I'm not... okay. Sorry."
"Why do we borrow?"
"Because... hmm. Because the two is really twelve if you take one ten from the next place."
"Ten from where?"
"From the four. Forty-two is four tens and two ones. Take one ten, now it's three tens and twelve ones."
"Oh! So twelve minus seven!"
"Yes! Five!"
"Why didn't you say that first?"
"I forgot I didn't know it once."

qa.q: What sum part did Jagdish first say couldn't be done?
qa.a: You can't take seven from two.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when Bhavna said she didn't understand?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and impatient, because borrowing seemed so easy to him that he couldn't see why she was lost.

qa.q: What change made Jagdish's teaching work?
qa.a: He explained the skipped step, that forty-two is four tens and two ones and one ten becomes ten ones, instead of just saying "borrow".

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel when Jagdish was shouting?
qa.a: Bhavna felt upset and lost, pointing out that he was shouting instead of explaining.

grounding: Shows an older child teaching his younger sister subtraction, skipping steps that seem obvious to him and getting frustrated until he explains them.

passage: I'm Shankar, and last summer I tried to teach my little sister Nandini chess. I thought it would be quick. I set up the board and said, "Okay, knights move in an L, bishops diagonally, and you need to control the centre." She looked at me like I was speaking French. I tried again, faster. "Just castle early and don't lose your queen." She moved a pawn backwards. I groaned, "No! Pawns can't do that!" She started crying and left. I was annoyed for an hour. Then I found my old chess book from when I was little. The first page just showed how a pawn moves. One piece. I'd forgotten I learned it that way. The next day I started Nandini with just pawns. She beat me.

qa.q: What did Nandini do that made Shankar groan?
qa.a: She moved a pawn backwards.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling when Nandini left crying?
qa.a: Shankar felt annoyed for an hour, thinking chess should be easy to learn, before remembering how it was learned step by step.

qa.q: What did Shankar change the next day, and why did it work?
qa.a: Shankar started with just pawns, one piece at a time, the way Shankar had learned from the old book, so Nandini wasn't overwhelmed.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel during the first lesson?
qa.a: Nandini felt confused and upset, as if Shankar were speaking French, and she cried and left.

grounding: An older child looks back on teaching a younger sister chess by skipping steps that seemed obvious, then remembering learning it one piece at a time.

passage:
Summer holiday note, stuck on the fridge by Nani.
This afternoon Gautam decided to teach Usha to tell the time. He pointed at the wall clock. "Easy. Short hand is hours, long hand is minutes, so that's quarter past three." Usha stared. "Where's the quarter?"
Gautam sighed loudly. "It's obvious. The three means fifteen." Usha's lip wobbled. "You said it's three!"
He threw up his hands. "She's not even trying, Nani."
I asked him, "Do you remember not knowing this?" He said no.
What I did next: I gave them a paper plate and crayons. Gautam made a clock with Usha, one hand at a time, starting with just the hours. By the end she could say "three o'clock", and they were both grinning.

qa.q: What did Gautam say the long hand shows?
qa.a: Gautam said the long hand is minutes.

qa.q: Why did Gautam get frustrated with Usha?
qa.a: Gautam felt impatient and frustrated, because the clock seemed obvious to him and he couldn't remember not knowing it.

qa.q: Why did the paper-plate clock work better?
qa.a: Making the clock one hand at a time, starting with hours, gave Usha the small steps Gautam had skipped.

qa.q: What was the lesson like for Usha?
qa.a: Usha felt lost and close to tears, confused by 'quarter' and a three that meant fifteen, until the steps got smaller.

grounding: Shows an older child teaching a younger sibling to tell time, skipping steps that seem obvious to him and getting frustrated.

passage:
Puja holidays, Saturday.
Today I taught Mridul chess. It was a disaster. I told him the rules really fast: horse goes in an L, bishop goes slanty, castle goes straight, don't leave your king in check. He moved the bishop straight and I said "No! Slanty!" about ten times. Then he cried and knocked the board over.
Baba asked me how long it took me to learn. I said I just knew. Baba said I learned when I was seven, it took a whole winter, and I cried too. I don't remember that at all.
Tomorrow I'll try one piece a day. Maybe just pawns first. And I won't say "it's easy", because it's easy for me, not for Mridul.
Anirban

qa.q: How did Anirban say the horse moves?
qa.a: Anirban said the horse goes in an L.

qa.q: Why did Anirban keep shouting 'No!' at Mridul?
qa.a: Anirban felt frustrated and impatient, because the rules felt so obvious that Mridul's mistakes seemed strange.

qa.q: What is Anirban's plan for tomorrow, and why is it better?
qa.a: One piece a day, starting with pawns, and not saying 'it's easy', because small steps suit a beginner.

qa.q: What might the chess lesson have felt like for Mridul?
qa.a: Mridul likely felt overwhelmed and upset, hearing many rules at once and being corrected again and again.

grounding: Shows an older child teaching a younger one chess, rushing rules that feel obvious and forgetting what it was like not to know them.

passage:
At the Sunday haat in Holi week, Lalit let his little sister Devika help at the tomato stall.
"Easy," he said. "Tomatoes are twenty a kilo, half a kilo is ten, so if they give fifty for a kilo and a half, you give twenty back." His fingers flicked through the coins.
Devika held a note in each hand and stared at the scale. "Which one is the kilo?"
"The kilo! On the scale!" Lalit's voice went sharp. "I just told you."
A customer was waiting. Devika's eyes filled.
Lalit stopped. He remembered Baba, years ago, showing him one coin at a time. It had taken a whole season.
He knelt. "Okay. Forget kilos. One basket, one ten-rupee coin. You give the basket, you take the coin. That's it."
Devika nodded and held out her hand to the customer.

qa.q: How much are tomatoes a kilo at the stall?
qa.a: Tomatoes are twenty a kilo.

qa.q: Why did Lalit's voice go sharp?
qa.a: Lalit felt impatient and flustered, because the sums were obvious to him and a customer was waiting.

qa.q: What did Lalit change, and why did it work?
qa.a: Lalit dropped the kilos and made it one basket for one coin, a single step Devika could manage.

qa.q: How did the first minutes at the stall feel for Devika?
qa.a: Devika felt confused and close to tears, holding notes she didn't understand while being told it was easy.

grounding: Shows an older child teaching a younger sibling at a market stall, skipping steps that seem obvious to him until he remembers learning slowly.

passage: On the morning before Tết, in their apartment in Houston, Bao was supposed to teach his little brother Mateo to fold paper lanterns for the window. Bao had made dozens. "Easy. Fold it, cut the lines, open it, glue it," he said, and his own lantern was done in a minute. Mateo stared at his crumpled sheet. "Fold it which way?" "Just fold it!" Mateo folded it the long way. "No, the other way! Why are you cutting there? I told you!" "You didn't tell me where," Mateo said, his lip wobbling. Bao threw down the scissors. "It's so obvious!" Mom looked over from the stove. "Was it obvious the first time you did it?" Bao opened his mouth, then remembered his first lantern, the one that fell apart.

qa.q: What was Bao supposed to teach Mateo?
qa.a: To fold paper lanterns for the window.

qa.q: Why does Bao get so frustrated?
qa.a: Having made dozens of lanterns, Bao can't remember not knowing how, so the steps feel obvious and Mateo's confusion makes him angry and impatient.

qa.q: What could Bao do to teach Mateo better?
qa.a: He could go slowly, show each fold and cut on his own sheet beside Mateo's, and remember his first lantern that fell apart.

qa.q: What is it like for Mateo when Bao says "It's so obvious"?
qa.a: Mateo feels lost and close to tears, because nobody told him which way to fold or where to cut.

grounding: Shows an older child teaching his younger brother, skipping steps that seem obvious to him and getting frustrated when the little one is lost.
